name: Faraday's candle: a whole course hiding in one flame
scope: Michael Faraday's Royal Institution Christmas Lectures on a single burning candle -- the most famous science lectures ever given, and the sub-strand's home base because every rung is watchable tonight with one candle. T1: Faraday spent SIX full lectures for a juvenile audience on one object, a burning candle, insisting there is no better door into the whole of science; the book everyone still reads was edited from the 1860-61 course by William Crookes (published 1861). T2: the wax is the fuel but nothing solid burns -- heat melts a pool and CAPILLARY ATTRACTION carries the liquid up the wick, in Faraday's words 'not in a careless way, but very beautifully in the very midst of the centre of action'; the wick is a pump, not the fuel. T3: the neat CUP at the top of a candle is built by the draught -- rising air cools the rim faster than the middle, so the edge stays solid and holds the melted wax; break the cup with a draught and the candle guts and runs. T4 (dinner-test payoff): blow the candle out cleverly, a white trail of vapour rises, and hold a lighted taper two or three inches off and 'a train of fire' runs back down the smoke to relight the wick -- proof that what burns is VAPOUR, not the wick. T5: the flame's yellow is not glowing gas -- it is SOLID PARTICLES OF CARBON heated white-hot inside the flame (the same soot that blacks a cold spoon); flames that make no solid particles, like hydrogen or alcohol, burn nearly invisible. T6: the flame is HOLLOW -- a dark cone of unburned vapour sits inside, and Faraday drew that vapour off through a bent glass tube and lit it at the far end: a second flame fed by the first. T7: a candle MAKES WATER -- 'that part of the product is just water, nothing but water'; a cold dry glass held over the flame fogs, because the hydrogen locked in the wax leaves as water vapour. T8: he then took that water apart again in front of the children with a battery, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen -- the candle's product decomposed on the lecture bench. T9: Lecture VI's closing analogy -- RESPIRATION is the candle's chemistry run slow: the child and the flame both take oxygen from the air and both give back carbonic acid; only speed and temperature differ. T10: Faraday's own start -- a bookbinder's apprentice with no schooling past the basics, who read the books he was binding, got tickets to Humphry Davy's lectures, bound up his own notes of them and sent the volume to Davy, and was taken on as his assistant. T11: the documented closing wish of 8 January 1861 -- that his young listeners 'may, in your generation, be fit to compare to a candle; that you may, like it, shine as lights to those about you'. T12: the modern extension -- in NASA microgravity experiments there is no convection to carry hot gas upward, so a candle flame is a small blue SPHERE, not a teardrop; the familiar flame shape is made by rising air, not by fire.
source: Grokipedia: The_Chemical_History_of_a_Candle (six lectures, first delivered 1848, repeated 1854 and 1860, compiled by William Crookes 1861 in Chemical News); Grokipedia: Royal_Institution_Christmas_Lectures; Grokipedia: Michael_Faraday. Primary text verified via Project Gutenberg full text (gutenberg.org/cache/epub/14474/pg14474.txt) -- exact quotes confirmed for capillary attraction ('very midst of the centre of action'), the cup formed by the air current, blowing out and relighting via 'a train of fire going through the air till it reaches the candle', solid luminous particles, and 'that part of the product is just water -- nothing but water'. Closing quote ('may, in your generation, be fit to compare to a candle... shine as lights to those about you') documented from the concluding lecture, 8 Jan 1861 (libquotes / todayinsci Faraday quotation collections). Microgravity spherical-flame rung: build stage must source directly from NASA candle-flame / FLEX experiment pages before authoring.
framing_note: The sub-strand's flagship DISCOVERY+MECHANISM ladder and the purest expression of the test-it-yourself soul -- every rung is a thing the kid can watch tonight with one candle and a cold spoon. ACCURACY RAIL (the one that matters): the famous book is the 1860-61 course published 1861 and edited by William Crookes; Faraday gave a candle course more than once (first 1848) and gave 19 Christmas Lecture series in all -- never date the BOOK to 1848 and never call this his only Christmas lectures. Second rail: the yellow light is incandescent SOLID CARBON, not 'glowing gas' -- say it right; and the microgravity rung must be sourced from NASA or dropped. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4 (relighting the flame through the smoke trail -- the trick the kid will run at the table) and T12 (a candle flame is a blue ball in space). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real graveyard of flame explanations -- phlogiston escaping the wax, the wick itself being the fuel, the wax burning as a solid, 'the oxygen glows' -- plus real adjacent lecturers and chemists (Davy, Tyndall, Crookes, Priestley, Lavoisier). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'the vapour is what burns' before asking what the smoke-trail relighting proves; describe the SCENE (the white trail, the taper held inches away) and let the conclusion be recalled. LANE BORDER: cooking flames, kitchen heat and flame-in-food belong to COOKING; combustion as thermodynamics belongs to the physics section -- this ladder owns the candle itself.

name: Lavoisier's sealed vessel and the death of phlogiston
scope: The balance that killed a respectable theory. T1: Antoine Lavoisier weighed everything. Sealing tin (and lead) with air inside a closed glass vessel and heating it, he found the metal came out HEAVIER -- while the sealed vessel as a whole weighed exactly what it had before; the extra weight came from inside the jar, not from nowhere. T2: the theory he was attacking was serious and taught everywhere -- Georg Stahl's PHLOGISTON, a fire-substance released by anything burning. Its fatal embarrassment: burned metals gained weight, and defenders patched the theory by giving phlogiston negative weight. T3 (dinner-test payoff): the twelve-day experiment -- Lavoisier kept mercury simmering in a sealed volume of air for twelve days; a red calx crusted the surface and the air shrank by roughly a fifth; the leftover air smothered a candle and killed a mouse. That missing fifth was the part that does the burning. T4: he then heated the red calx by itself and got the missing air BACK, and the mercury back too -- the ledger closed in both directions, which is what a story about escaping fire-stuff could never do. T5: Joseph Priestley got that gas first in 1774 by focusing sunlight through a burning lens onto mercury calx (a mouse lived far longer in it, a candle blazed); Carl Wilhelm Scheele had made it even earlier, around 1771-72, but published in 1777. Priestley called it 'dephlogisticated air' and defended phlogiston to his death. T6: Lavoisier named it OXYGENE, 'acid-former', because he believed every acid contained it -- and he was wrong: hydrochloric acid contains no oxygen at all. The man who killed one wrong theory built his own mistake into the name we still use. T7: the conservation statement, from the Traite elementaire de chimie (1789) -- nothing is created in the operations of art or of nature, and there is an equal quantity of matter before and after every operation. T8: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier translated Richard Kirwan's 'Essay on Phlogiston' (1787) into French so the French chemists could publish the refutation alongside it, translated Priestley and Cavendish for the lab, and engraved the plates of the apparatus. T9: he paid for the laboratory with the job that killed him -- he was a tax farmer of the Ferme generale, arrested and guillotined on 8 May 1794; Lagrange's remark, reported through Delambre, was that it took only an instant to cut off that head and a hundred years might not produce another like it. T10: what the law means on a school bench -- burn steel wool on a balance and it gets HEAVIER, burn a candle in an open jar and it seems to lose mass; the law only holds when you count the GASES, which is exactly why sealed vessels were the breakthrough. T11: the honest modern caveat a bright 15-year-old should hear -- mass is not perfectly conserved. Because energy has mass, a chemical reaction really does change the total by parts in a billion, far below any balance ever built; in nuclear reactions the change is enormous. Conservation of mass is a superb approximation, not a law of the universe. T12: how a wrong theory actually dies -- phlogiston lost because the balance produced NUMBERS an argument could not talk around, and even so its greatest experimentalist, Priestley, never converted.
source: Grokipedia: Antoine_Lavoisier (sealed-vessel tin/lead/phosphorus calcination with precise weighings; mercury-calx work 1777; oxygen named 1778 from Greek 'acid producer'; ice calorimeter with Laplace); Grokipedia: Conservation_of_mass (formulated 1789, sealed-vessel demonstration); Grokipedia: Phlogiston_theory; Grokipedia: Chemical_revolution; Grokipedia: Oxygen; Grokipedia: Marie-Anne_Paulze_Lavoisier (translated Kirwan's Essay on Phlogiston 1787, translated Priestley/Watt/Kirwan, engraved apparatus plates). Lagrange remark attributed via Delambre; execution 8 May 1794 after arrest of the Ferme generale tax farmers -- corroborated via general reference search. Build stage should re-verify Priestley 1774 / Scheele c.1771-77 priority and the exact 1789 Traite wording against Grokipedia first.
framing_note: The sub-strand's REVERSAL flagship: phlogiston told honestly as the live consensus of serious, competent men, beaten not by argument but by a balance. THREE ACCURACY RAILS, all binding: (a) Lavoisier did NOT discover oxygen -- Scheele made it first, Priestley published first, Lavoisier explained and named it; no rung may imply discovery. (b) 'Rien ne se perd, rien ne se cree, tout se transforme' is a LATER popular paraphrase, not a Lavoisier sentence -- if the bank quotes him, quote the 1789 Traite wording. (c) He was executed as a TAX FARMER, not for his chemistry, and the 'the Republic has no need of scientists' line attributed to the tribunal is unverified -- the bank must NOT use it. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 (twelve days of simmering mercury and the air shrank by a fifth) and T11 (mass isn't really conserved, just almost). DISTRACTOR MINE: the richest in the sub-strand -- phlogiston, caloric, the four elements, 'the metal absorbed fire particles', 'the fire drove out moisture' -- plus real adjacent names (Priestley, Scheele, Cavendish, Stahl, Black, Boyle, Berthollet). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'air combines with the metal' before asking what the sealed vessel showed; give the SCENE (sealed glass, heavier tin, unchanged total) and let the conclusion be knowledge. LANE BORDER: the Terror as political episode is HISTORY's -- T9 is one closing rung on the cost of the man, never a Revolution tour; the Lavoisier-Laplace ice calorimeter is owned by this sub-strand's endothermic/exothermic ladder, not repeated here.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank likely covers the French Revolution / Reign of Terror and may name Lavoisier's execution. This ladder keys the CHEMISTRY (sealed vessel, phlogiston's fall, the oxygen-naming mistake, the balance as the decider) and confines the guillotine to a single closing rung framed by Lagrange's remark, not a Revolution narrative.

name: Flame tests: the fingerprint in the fire
scope: How a colour became a NAME. T1: fireworks are chemistry writing in the sky -- strontium salts burn red, copper blue-green, sodium yellow, barium green; the colour is not a pigment surviving the fire, it is the ELEMENT itself giving off light. T2: table salt on a clean wire held in a gas flame flares orange-yellow every single time -- the kitchen-grade flame test, and the same sodium yellow that made old street lamps drain the colour out of parked cars. T3: Robert Bunsen's burner (mid-1850s, built with his university mechanic Peter Desaga) exists BECAUSE of this problem -- he needed a nearly colourless, non-luminous flame, since the sooty yellow of an ordinary gas lamp drowned the colours he was hunting. The instrument was designed around the obstacle. T4: in 1859-60 Bunsen and the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff put a prism between the flame and the eye, turning a smear of colour into a set of sharp LINES -- and the same element gave the same lines every time, in any mineral, at any concentration. T5 (dinner-test payoff): on 10 May 1860, in a residue boiled down from the Maxquelle mineral spring at Bad Duerkheim, two blue lines appeared that belonged to no known element -- Bunsen named it CAESIUM after Latin caesius, 'sky blue'. In 1861 two deep-red lines in the same water gave RUBIDIUM, from rubidus, 'darkest red'. The first elements in history found by their LIGHT before anyone held a grain of them. T6: the brute-force half nobody puts on the poster -- to get a weighable quantity of caesium salts for chemical confirmation, Bunsen boiled down on the order of forty tonnes of mineral water. T7: the mechanism in a paragraph -- heat kicks an atom's electron up to a higher level; falling back, it emits a photon of one definite energy, which is one definite colour. Different elements have differently spaced levels, so the pattern is a fingerprint. Niels Bohr supplied the WHY fifty years later: the fingerprint was in daily use long before anyone understood it. T8: contamination is the enemy the textbooks skip -- a trace of sodium from a fingerprint, dust or sweat floods any flame yellow, so Bunsen viewed flames through blue cobalt glass to filter the sodium out and see the potassium lilac hiding behind it. T9: Kirchhoff matched his bright sodium lines against the dark lines Fraunhofer had mapped in sunlight in 1814 -- the same element, in emission on the bench and in absorption in the Sun. T10 (REVERSAL): in 1835 Auguste Comte had chosen the chemical composition of the stars as his standard example of knowledge forever beyond human reach -- 'inconceivable', he wrote, that we should ever study it by any means whatever. Within about twenty-five years a prism and a flame had it.

Rubidium 1861, deep-red lines ~780.0 and 794.8 nm. Comte's 1835 claim and its refutation: J. B. Hearnshaw, 'Auguste Comte's Blunder', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 13 (2010) 90 (ADS abstract), plus Comte, Cours de philosophie positive (1835), 19th lesson.
framing_note: DISCOVERY + MECHANISM ladder; the whole payoff is that a COLOUR turned out to be a NAME, and that a spectroscope beat a philosopher's certainty. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) the burner is Bunsen's design executed by his mechanic Peter Desaga and built on earlier gas-burner work -- do not write 'Bunsen invented the gas burner'; (b) caesium 10 May 1860 and rubidium 1861, BOTH from the Duerkheim mineral water, both found spectroscopically BEFORE isolation; (c) Comte's line concerns the chemical composition of stars in Cours de philosophie positive (1835) -- quote it as a confident expert impossibility-claim overturned by a test, and do NOT inflate it into a general sneer at philosophy (that lane is PHILOSOPHY's). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T5 (an element discovered as two blue lines and named for the colour) and T6 (forty tonnes of spa water for a pinch of salt). DISTRACTOR MINE: real elements with real flame colours (lithium crimson, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, boron green, barium green) and real adjacent scientists (Fraunhofer, Angstrom, Talbot, Herschel, Huggins, Ramsay). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never name the colour and the element in the same stem -- if the stem says 'sky blue', caesium cannot be the asked answer. LANE BORDER: stellar spectroscopy, helium-found-in-the-Sun and star composition belong to the EARTHSPACE section's ladders -- T9/T10 here key the chemist's flame and Comte's refuted claim, one rung each, and must not become an astronomy tour.

name: Two pencils and a battery: electrolysis takes matter apart
scope: Electricity as the tool that pries open what fire cannot. T1: sharpen a pencil at both ends, stand two of them in a glass of water with a pinch of baking soda dissolved, touch them to a 9-volt battery -- bubbles climb off both leads, and about TWICE as much gas collects at the negative one. The formula H2O made visible in a kitchen glass. T2: 1800 -- within weeks of Volta announcing his pile, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle in London ran its current through water and collected the two gases separately: the first time electricity was used to pull a compound apart. T3 (dinner-test payoff): 1807 -- Humphry Davy melted caustic potash and drove a huge battery through it, and shining metallic globules appeared at the negative wire, skittered across the surface and burst into lilac flame. POTASSIUM: a metal so reactive nobody had ever seen it, because it never occurs alone. T4: he repeated the trick at a stunning pace -- sodium in the same year, then calcium, magnesium, strontium, barium and boron in 1808. Six new elements in about two years, because electricity beats heat at prying apart the most tightly held compounds. T5: 1834 -- Faraday's laws of electrolysis: the amount of substance freed at an electrode is proportional to the QUANTITY OF ELECTRICITY passed, and for a fixed charge the amounts of different substances go by their chemical equivalents. Chemistry could now be measured in charge. T6: Faraday needed vocabulary for a science that did not exist yet, so he wrote to the Cambridge polymath William Whewell, who coined ELECTRODE, ANODE, CATHODE, ION, ANION, CATION and ELECTROLYTE in 1834 -- the words on every battery label were invented in a letter exchange. T7: the mechanism, and the reason the demo needs salt -- inside the liquid the charge is carried by IONS physically travelling to the electrodes, not by electrons swimming; genuinely pure distilled water barely conducts at all, which a kid can test by running the demo with distilled water first and watching almost nothing happen. T8: how precious aluminium once was -- in 1884 the fanciest thing America could set atop the Washington Monument was a 100-ounce cast aluminium pyramid, and Napoleon III had served honoured banquet guests on aluminium while lesser guests made do with gold. T9: 1886 -- Charles Martin Hall, 22, at Oberlin College, and Paul Heroult, 22, in France, independently dissolved alumina in molten cryolite and electrolysed it; within a generation the precious metal was a disposable can. Same element, same chemistry, price collapsed. T10: the ledger runs backwards too -- a fuel cell is electrolysis in reverse, recombining hydrogen and oxygen to give back electricity and pure water; Apollo's fuel cells supplied the crew with both their power and their drinking water.
source: Grokipedia: Electrolysis_of_water; Grokipedia: Electrolysis (Nicholson & Carlisle 1800 with Volta's pile); Grokipedia: Voltaic_pile; Grokipedia: Electrochemistry (Davy 1807 electrolysing molten potassium hydroxide in a platinum spoon, then sodium hydroxide); Grokipedia: Faraday's_laws_of_electrolysis (1832-34); Grokipedia: William_Whewell / Cathode / Anode / Ion / Electrolyte (Whewell coined electrode, anode, cathode, ion, anion, cation, electrolyte at Faraday's request, 1834, confirmed in Faraday's May 1834 letter); Grokipedia: Hall-Heroult_process and Charles_Martin_Hall (first successful electrolysis 23 Feb 1886, alumina in molten cryolite, carbon anode); Grokipedia: History_of_aluminium and Washington_Monument (aluminium apex 8.9 in, 100 oz, 1884, ~$225; Napoleon III's aluminium cutlery 1855). Apollo fuel-cell water rung to be re-sourced at build stage.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder anchored to the single cheapest demo in the sub-strand -- two pencils, a battery, a glass of water. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Davy did NOT electrolyse a water solution to get potassium; he electrolysed MOLTEN (slightly damp) caustic potash -- in water you only get hydrogen, and getting this wrong destroys the point of the rung. (b) The 2:1 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio is by VOLUME and the collected oxygen usually reads a little low (it dissolves and attacks the electrode) -- write 'about twice', and put the honest wrinkle in context. (c) Whewell coined the terms at Faraday's request; credit both men. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 (globules of a brand-new metal catching fire on the wire) and T9 (two 22-year-olds turned a metal more precious than gold into a soda can). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent figures and rival claims (Volta, Ritter, Berzelius, Cruickshank, Wollaston, Deville's chemical aluminium process) plus real wrong mechanisms ('the battery creates new elements', 'electrons swim through the water', 'enough heat can free any metal'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never state the 2:1 ratio in a stem that asks what the two pencil-bubble streams reveal. LANE BORDER: batteries as electricity, circuits and Volta's pile as a physics story belong to the PHYSICS section -- this ladder owns the CHEMICAL decomposition and the elements it delivered; the aluminium PRICE story is economics-flavoured but stays here because the cause is the electrolysis.

name: Catalysts: changed by nothing, changing everything
scope: A CONCEPT ladder on the strangest bargain in chemistry -- a substance that transforms a reaction and walks away unaltered. T1 (dinner-test payoff): pour drugstore hydrogen peroxide on a piece of raw liver and it erupts into foam; pour it on liver that has been BOILED first and almost nothing happens. Same peroxide, same meat -- what the fresh liver has is the enzyme CATALASE, and heat has wrecked its shape. T2: catalase is among the fastest enzymes known -- a single molecule tears apart on the order of tens of millions of hydrogen-peroxide molecules per second, close to the hard limit set by how fast molecules can even arrive. T3: 1823 -- Johann Wolfgang Doebereiner found that a jet of hydrogen aimed at spongy platinum burst into flame with no spark, no match and no heating, and the platinum came out unchanged and reusable. His 'Doebereiner lamp' was sold as a pocket lighter for decades before reliable matches existed. T4: 1835 -- Joens Jacob Berzelius gathered Doebereiner's platinum results and a pile of similar oddities under one name, CATALYSIS: an agent that hastens a reaction while emerging unaltered in quantity and quality. Naming the class was the discovery. T5: the mechanism, and the rail that kills the magic -- a catalyst supplies NO energy and cannot make an impossible reaction happen. It opens a lower-energy PATH to the same destination, a lower pass over the same mountains, so a change that would take years takes seconds. It moves the speed, never the endpoint. T6: Irving Langmuir showed where the action is: on the SURFACE. Gas molecules stick to the metal, their bonds stretch and weaken, they meet a neighbour and leave -- which is why catalysts are built as sponges, powders and honeycombs, because surface area is the entire game. T7: the catalytic converter -- a ceramic honeycomb washcoated with platinum, palladium and rhodium, required on American light-duty cars from the 1975 model year, turning carbon monoxide and unburned fuel into carbon dioxide and water, and in the later three-way design turning nitrogen oxides back into plain nitrogen. T8: catalysts can be MURDERED -- lead coats and deactivates the platinum-group metals, so a single tank of leaded petrol permanently ruins a converter. 'Catalyst poisoning' is the named reason leaded fuel had to go. T9: the one that feeds the world -- Fritz Haber demonstrated it at lab scale in 1909 and Carl Bosch made it industrial at BASF by 1913: an IRON catalyst under great pressure lets the inert nitrogen of ordinary air become ammonia. Vaclav Smil's estimate is that the resulting fertiliser underwrites roughly 40-50% of the world's food supply. T10: your own body is run by catalysts -- every enzyme is one, and the reason a high fever is dangerous is exactly the reason boiled liver goes flat: shape is function, and heat destroys the shape.

framing_note: CONCEPT/THEME ladder -- the analytic backbone of this sub-strand: ONE idea (a lower path, not a bigger push) displayed across an enzyme, a pocket lighter, a car exhaust and the world's fertiliser. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) a catalyst does NOT supply energy and does NOT change where a reaction ends up -- only how fast it gets there; any rung implying otherwise is simply wrong, and 'it lowers the temperature the reaction needs' is the subtly-wrong cousin worth using as a DISTRACTOR rather than an answer. (b) Haber demonstrated the lab process (1909), Bosch engineered it (by 1913) -- credit both, never 'the Haber process was invented by Haber-Bosch'. (c) Smil's 40-50% figure is an ESTIMATE: attribute it to him, never state it as a measured constant. (d) any surface-area number for a converter honeycomb must be sourced at build stage or dropped. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1 (boiled liver does nothing) and T8 (one tank of the wrong fuel kills a converter forever). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent chemistry (a reactant consumed, a solvent, an inhibitor, an initiator, raw heat, raw pressure) and real names (Berzelius, Doebereiner, Ostwald, Langmuir, Sabatier, Haber, Bosch, Mittasch). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never say 'the enzyme is destroyed by heat' in the stem that asks why boiled liver does nothing. LANE BORDER: kitchen enzymes and fermentation as CRAFT (rennet, meat tenderiser, yeast in dough) belong to COOKING -- here enzymes appear only as the biological case of the catalysis mechanism.
history_overlap: COOKING bank owns kitchen enzymes and fermentation-as-craft; this ladder uses liver + peroxide and yeast strictly as catalysis demonstrations, never as cuisine. If a sister science sub-strand builds a Haber-Bosch topic of its own, T9 here must key ONLY the iron catalyst; the nitrates-and-WWI / Haber's gas-warfare story belongs to the HISTORY bank.

name: Red cabbage, litmus, and the ladder of ten
scope: A CONCEPT ladder on acidity built around the most kid-runnable experiment in chemistry. T1: boil chopped red cabbage, strain off the deep purple water, and you are holding an instrument -- a spoonful of vinegar turns it PINK, a spoonful of baking-soda solution turns it BLUE-GREEN, a strong drain cleaner takes it to yellow. The anthocyanin pigments physically change shape as they gain or lose a hydrogen ion. T2: the juice does not read two states but a whole staircase -- red around pH 1-2, pink at 3, violet 4-6, blue 7-8, green 9-11, yellow at 12. One supermarket vegetable is a universal indicator. T3: Robert Boyle did this on purpose and wrote it down -- his 'Experiments and Considerations Touching Colours' (1664) systematically tested plant dyes such as syrup of violets and lichen-derived litmus against acids and alkalis, turning a curiosity into a repeatable TEST anyone could run. (Litmus itself is far older: its use is credited to Arnaldus de Villa Nova around 1300.) T4: 1909 -- S. P. L. Soerensen, working in the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory in Copenhagen and needing to control acidity in beer, invented the pH scale so that acidity could be said in one number. T5: the number is LOGARITHMIC and that is the entire point -- each step of 1 is a factor of TEN in hydrogen-ion concentration, so lemon juice near pH 2 is a hundred times more acidic than tomato juice near 4, and a thousand times more than coffee at 5. T6: your own stomach runs at roughly pH 1.5-3.5 -- acid that would attack metal, held off your own flesh only by a mucus layer your body rebuilds continuously. T7 (REVERSAL, dinner-test payoff): 1884 -- Svante Arrhenius proposed that acids work by releasing hydrogen ions and that salts split into free charged particles in water. His Uppsala examiners found free ions in solution so implausible that they passed the dissertation with the lowest grade they could give it. He won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the same idea. T8: 1923 -- Johannes Broensted and Thomas Martin Lowry, independently, generalised it: an acid DONATES a proton and a base ACCEPTS one, no solvent required. This rescued ammonia, a strong base containing no OH at all -- the exact case Arrhenius's definition could not handle. T9: neutralisation, watched -- vinegar plus baking soda fizzes because the acid and the carbonate first make carbonic acid, which instantly falls apart into water and carbon dioxide; the foam is the gas leaving. Run it on a kitchen scale in an open cup and the mass DROPS; run it in a sealed bag and it does not. T10: strength versus concentration, the distinction that trips everyone -- hydrochloric acid is STRONG because it releases its proton essentially completely, while vinegar's acetic acid is WEAK because most of it stays intact; a dilute strong acid can be gentler than a concentrated weak one, because pH measures what is actually loose, not what is in the bottle.

framing_note: CONCEPT ladder and the sub-strand's kitchen heart -- every rung is testable with one cabbage, a lemon and a box of baking soda, so frame T1/T2/T9 as invitations, not descriptions. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) the cabbage colours are a RANGE, not 'pink means acid, green means base' -- teach the staircase or the topic is a lie; (b) Boyle SYSTEMATISED plant indicators, he did not invent litmus (credited far earlier to Arnaldus de Villa Nova, c.1300) -- do not let a rung crown Boyle the inventor; (c) pH is defined on hydrogen-ion activity and 0 and 14 are not hard walls -- never teach 'the scale runs 0 to 14' as a law of nature; (d) never define a base as 'a thing containing OH' -- T8 exists precisely to correct that. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1/T2 (one vegetable is an entire instrument) and T7 (the dissertation that barely passed and won a Nobel). DISTRACTOR MINE: real wrong-but-live ideas (Lavoisier's oxygen-is-the-acid-maker error, acidity as a property of the salt, 'acids are simply things that burn skin', an indicator 'adding' acid to what it measures) plus real adjacent chemists (Boyle, Lavoisier, Davy, Liebig, Ostwald, G. N. Lewis). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never state 'each step is ten times' in the stem that asks how much stronger lemon is than tomato. LANE BORDER: pickling, sourdough sourness and cabbage as FOOD belong to COOKING -- here the cabbage is an INSTRUMENT and never an ingredient; ocean acidification and climate framing stay out of this ladder entirely.
history_overlap: COOKING bank owns fermentation, pickling and food acidity as craft. This ladder must treat cabbage juice strictly as a measuring instrument; no rung may key a food outcome.

name: Rust: fire running in slow motion
scope: Oxidation you can watch over weeks instead of seconds. T1: three nails, three jars -- one in dry air over a drying agent, one in water that has been boiled to drive out its air and sealed under a film of oil, one in ordinary tap water half-exposed to the air. Only the third rusts. Iron needs oxygen AND water together, and either alone does nothing. T2: rust and fire have the SAME partner -- iron joining with oxygen. Steel wool flaring in a flame and a gate rusting through a winter are one reaction at wildly different speeds; rust simply never gets hot enough to glow. T3 (dinner-test payoff): burn steel wool on a kitchen scale and it gets HEAVIER, which feels backwards for something that looks destroyed. The oxygen it pulled from the air has weight -- the same ledger Lavoisier used to kill phlogiston. T4: rust is the traitor among oxides. The iron oxides it forms are flaky and porous, so they shed and expose fresh metal and the attack never stops. Aluminium's oxide does the opposite -- a tight, invisible film that seals the surface within seconds, which is why aluminium foil does not quietly dissolve in a damp drawer. Same chemistry, opposite outcome, and the difference is the STRUCTURE of the oxide. T5: the Statue of Liberty's copper skin is only about 2.4 mm thick -- barely two coins -- and after more than a century in salt air she has lost only a few percent of it, because that green patina is a sealing layer, not a wound. T6: rusting is ELECTRICAL. It runs as a tiny battery on the metal's own surface: one patch behaves as anode and gives up iron, another as cathode, and water carries the ions between them. That is why salt water is so brutal -- salt makes the water a far better conductor, which is why a car rusts fastest where the road is salted. T7: the trick that exploits the battery -- bolt blocks of zinc to a ship's steel hull or into a water heater and the ZINC corrodes instead, because zinc gives up electrons more readily than iron (-0.76 V against -0.44 V). They are called sacrificial anodes and are replaced on a schedule; galvanising is the same bargain painted on as a coating.
source: Grokipedia: Rust; Grokipedia: Corrosion_engineering (anodic Fe -> Fe2+ + 2e-, coupled cathodic oxygen reduction); Grokipedia: Galvanic_anode and Sacrificial_metal (zinc/magnesium/aluminium anodes more anodic than iron; zinc -0.76 V vs iron -0.44 V vs SHE); Grokipedia: Galvanization; Grokipedia: Passivation_(chemistry) and 1100_aluminium_alloy (self-passivating Al2O3 film forming rapidly on exposure); Grokipedia: Patina and Conservation-restoration_of_the_Statue_of_Liberty (copper sheets ~2.4 mm; protective patina of copper carbonate/sulfate compounds; corrosion loss on the order of a few percent over the first century).
framing_note: MECHANISM ladder built entirely out of things a kid can set up in jars on a windowsill and check for a fortnight -- frame T1 as an experiment to RUN, not a fact to memorise. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) rust needs oxygen AND water -- a nail in genuinely dry air does not rust, and a nail in properly deoxygenated water does not either; state both halves or the T1 rung is false; (b) rust is a family of hydrated iron oxides, not one clean compound -- write 'iron oxides', never present Fe2O3 as the tidy whole answer; (c) the Statue's few-percent-loss figure and the 2.4 mm skin should be attributed to the conservation record, not asserted as a fresh measurement. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 (burnt steel wool weighs MORE) and T7 (ships are saved by a metal that agrees to be eaten). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent chemistry (paint as a pure barrier versus cathodic protection, chromium's passive film in stainless steel, silver tarnish as a sulfide not an oxide, verdigris) and real wrong-but-plausible causes ('air alone', 'acid rain alone', 'metal fatigue', 'the paint wore off'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem mention oxygen's weight before asking why burnt steel wool gains mass. LANE BORDER: the hand warmer as deliberately hurried rust is OWNED by this sub-strand's endothermic/exothermic ladder -- do not repeat it here; conservation of mass belongs to the Lavoisier ladder, so T3 here keys only the counter-intuitive WEIGHT GAIN.

name: Heat you can hold: endothermic and exothermic in your palm
scope: A CONCEPT ladder where every rung is something the kid has physically held. T1: squeeze an instant cold pack and it plunges toward 0 C in seconds -- nothing frozen inside, nothing burning. An inner pouch of water bursts over solid AMMONIUM NITRATE, and the dissolving PULLS heat out of the pack and out of your hand. Nothing makes cold; cold is heat leaving. T2 (dinner-test payoff): the disposable hand warmer is the same idea run the other way, and its secret is faintly embarrassing -- it is iron powder RUSTING on purpose, hurried along by salt, water, charcoal and vermiculite, releasing about 1.7 kilocalories per gram of iron over hours. Tearing the outer wrapper does not start a machine; it lets oxygen in. T3: the rule underneath both -- BREAKING a bond always costs energy and FORMING one always releases it; whether a change warms your hand or chills it depends only on which side of that arithmetic wins. There is no third kind. T4: the reusable heat pad is a trap sprung on command -- a supersaturated sodium acetate solution sits liquid far below the temperature at which it ought to have crystallised, until you click the small metal disc and a wave of white crystals races through it, giving out heat as it goes solid. Boil the pack and the trap resets, hundreds of times. T5: the demonstration that makes ICE out of a reaction -- barium hydroxide octahydrate stirred with ammonium thiocyanate in a beaker runs so far endothermic that the beaker freezes itself to a wet wooden block. Two solids, mixed, and frost forms on the outside of the glass. T6: 1782-83 -- Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace built an ICE CALORIMETER, sat a guinea pig in the inner chamber, and measured the animal's warmth by how much ice it melted; the heat per unit of carbon dioxide matched ordinary burning. Breathing is slow combustion, and they measured it in melted ice. T7: the far end of exothermic -- Hans Goldschmidt's aluminothermic reaction (1893, patented 1895): aluminium powder and iron oxide, once started, exceed 2,000 C and pour out molten iron. Since 1899 it has welded railway rails in place, outdoors, with no power supply -- because aluminium wants oxygen more than iron does, and simply takes it.
source: Grokipedia: Endothermic_process; Grokipedia: Ice_pack (ammonium nitrate dissolution, ~25 kJ/mol absorbed, near 0 C); Grokipedia: Hand_warmer (iron powder, water, activated charcoal, vermiculite, salt; 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3; ~1.7 kcal per gram of iron; supersaturated sodium acetate crystallisation type reusable by boiling); Grokipedia: Heating_pad; Grokipedia: Antoine_Lavoisier and Indirect_calorimetry (ice calorimeter with Laplace c.1782-83, guinea pig in a wire basket surrounded by ice, up to ten hours, heat from ice melted, respiration as slow combustion); Grokipedia: Aluminothermic_reaction and Exothermic_welding (Goldschmidt 1893, patented 1895; Fe2O3 + 2Al -> 2Fe + Al2O3, >2000 C; first rail welding 1899 on Essen tram tracks; Goldschmidt Thermit Company New York 1904).
framing_note: CONCEPT ladder; the through-line is that hot and cold are the SAME bookkeeping read in two directions. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) 'endothermic' properly covers physical processes such as DISSOLVING and CRYSTALLISING, not only bond-breaking reactions -- the cold pack is a dissolution, and the bank must not call it a chemical reaction; (b) cold is not a substance and nothing 'produces cold' -- if a stem or answer ever says so, it is a defect; (c) the ~1.7 kcal/g and ~25 kJ/mol figures are sourced -- keep them exactly or drop them, never round them into invention; (d) the barium hydroxide / ammonium thiocyanate demo releases ammonia and uses a toxic barium salt: present it as something WATCHED in a lab, never as 'try this at home'. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T2 (your hand warmer is rust) and T4 (a liquid that freezes when you click a disc, and gets HOT doing it). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent processes that look like the answer (evaporative cooling, latent heat of fusion, salt melting ice on a road, plain combustion, acid-base neutralisation) and real names (Joseph Black on latent heat, Laplace, Joule, Hess). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem mention rust or iron before asking what is inside a hand warmer. LANE BORDER: latent heat, heat engines and the thermodynamic laws belong to the PHYSICS section; the hand-warmer-as-rust fact is OWNED here, so this sub-strand's rust ladder must not repeat it, and the Lavoisier balance story is owned by the phlogiston ladder -- T6 here keys only the ice calorimeter.

name: Joseph Black's 'fixed air': the gas you can pour
scope: The first gas anyone ever pinned down as a distinct chemical substance. T1 (dinner-test payoff): fizz vinegar and baking soda in a jug, then TIP the invisible contents -- not the liquid -- down a paper chute onto a lit candle, and the flame goes out. Carbon dioxide is denser than air, so a gas can be poured like water. T2: 1754 -- Joseph Black in Edinburgh heated magnesia alba (magnesium carbonate) and found the residue weighed LESS; the missing weight had left as a gas he named 'fixed air', and he could put it back and reconstitute the original substance. Before Black, air was one thing; after him, a gas was a specific chemical with an account that had to balance. T3: Black's test is still the school test -- bubble the gas through clear limewater and it turns MILKY as solid chalk precipitates. You can watch a gas turn into a rock. T4: the same gas smothers a flame and will not support breathing, which is why it fills fire extinguishers -- and why it is genuinely lethal in the bottom of a silo, a well or an old brewery vat, because it sits exactly where a person has to stand. T5: 1767 -- Joseph Priestley, living beside a brewery in Leeds, hung a bowl of water over the fermenting vats where fixed air lay thick and invented CARBONATED WATER, later refining it with chalk and acid. He took no money from it; Johann Jacob Schweppe built the business. T6: solid carbon dioxide never melts at ordinary pressure -- at about -78.5 C dry ice goes straight from solid to gas, and the 'smoke' pouring off it is not the gas at all but water vapour from the room condensing in the cold plume.
source: Grokipedia: Joseph_Black (1754 magnesia alba experiments, 'fixed air' lost on heating and restorable, precise weighings distinguishing magnesia alba from calx of lime; fixed air extinguishes flames and is absorbed by limewater); Grokipedia: Carbon_dioxide; Grokipedia: Carbonated_water and Timeline_of_chemistry (Priestley 1767, water suspended over brewery fermentation vats, later chalk + sulfuric acid method; Schweppe commercialisation); Grokipedia: Carbonic_acid; Grokipedia: Chemical_revolution. Dry-ice sublimation point to be re-verified at build stage.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder for the moment 'air' stopped being one thing. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Black identified fixed air by WEIGHING -- he is the quantitative precedent Lavoisier built on, not a footnote to him, and no rung may hand Black's result to Lavoisier; (b) the fog rolling off dry ice is condensed WATER vapour from the room, not visible CO2 -- this is the corrected-misconception rung and must be stated plainly; (c) CO2 asphyxiation in cellars, silos and vats is a real documented hazard -- present it as a fact, never as something to test. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1 (pouring an invisible gas onto a candle flame) and T5 (soda water was invented over a brewery vat by a man who never charged for it). DISTRACTOR MINE: the eighteenth-century gas menagerie under its real period names -- 'inflammable air' (hydrogen), 'mephitic air' (nitrogen), 'dephlogisticated air' (oxygen), phlogiston itself -- plus real adjacent names (Priestley, Cavendish, Scheele, Daniel Rutherford, van Helmont who coined the word 'gas'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never say the gas is denser than air in the stem that asks why the poured gas snuffs the candle. LANE BORDER: fizzy drinks as beverage/craft belong to COOKING (this rung keys the DISCOVERY, not the drink); CO2 in the greenhouse effect belongs to the earth/climate ladders and must stay out of this ladder entirely; Black's latent-heat work belongs to the PHYSICS section.
history_overlap: COOKING bank owns carbonated drinks as beverage craft -- T5 here keys Priestley's invention moment only. The climate/greenhouse role of CO2 belongs to the science bank's earth/climate ladders and is excluded here by design.

name: Cold light: glow sticks and luminol
scope: Light made by a reaction instead of by heat. T1: snap a glow stick and you are breaking a thin glass ampoule of hydrogen peroxide into a solution of an oxalate ester; the energy released goes straight into a DYE molecule, and the dye alone decides the colour -- every colour of stick runs the same reaction. T2 (dinner-test payoff): temperature is the volume knob, and a kid can test it tonight -- drop a glow stick in hot water and it blazes and burns out fast; put an identical one in the freezer and it dims but lasts for days. The total light is roughly fixed; heat only spends it faster. T3: 1928 -- H. O. Albrecht reported that the compound now called luminol glows blue when oxidised in alkaline hydrogen peroxide. Forensic labs spray it in darkened rooms because the IRON in haemoglobin catalyses that glow, so bloodstains scrubbed off a floor years earlier light up. T4: the caveat that keeps it science instead of crime television -- luminol is NOT a blood test. Household bleach, copper, and plant peroxidases (horseradish is the textbook offender) all set it off, and the spray can damage the DNA evidence investigators were hoping to type. The glow is a lead, never a verdict. T5: the family it belongs to, and the confusions worth killing -- chemiluminescence makes its own light from a reaction; FLUORESCENCE (a highlighter under a UV lamp) only re-emits light it is being given right now and stops the instant the lamp goes off; PHOSPHORESCENCE (glow-in-the-dark stars) stores that borrowed light and leaks it slowly. Three different things people call 'glowing'.

Albrecht 1928 reported the blue glow on oxidation in alkaline hydrogen peroxide; iron in haemoglobin catalyses; false positives from copper and iron ions, sodium hypochlorite bleach, and plant peroxidases such as horseradish); Grokipedia: Chemiluminescence (peroxyoxalate system developed by Edwin A. Chandross at Bell Laboratories 1963; commercialised as glow sticks by American Cyanamid in the 1970s); Grokipedia: Horseradish_peroxidase; Grokipedia: Kastle-Meyer_test; Grokipedia: Forensic_serology.
framing_note: MECHANISM gem with an honest-caveat spine; deliberately short because the sub-strand's heavy lifting sits in the candle, Lavoisier, catalyst and pH ladders. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) chemiluminescence is light WITHOUT appreciable heat -- never describe a glow stick as burning; (b) luminol gives a PRESUMPTIVE result only, and the false-positive list (bleach, copper, horseradish and other plant peroxidases) must appear in the ladder or the topic degenerates into crime-TV; (c) if the build wants an invention rung, credit Edwin Chandross's 1963 peroxyoxalate work at Bell Labs and American Cyanamid's 1970s commercialisation -- do not attribute the glow stick to a lone hobbyist. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T2 (the freezer-versus-hot-water trick with two party glow sticks). DISTRACTOR MINE: the real adjacent light phenomena that T5 exists to separate -- fluorescence under UV, phosphorescence in glow-in-the-dark plastic, incandescence in a filament, an LED's electroluminescence -- these are exactly the confusions worth killing, and they make honest, live choices. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never mention iron or haemoglobin in the stem that asks why luminol reveals a scrubbed bloodstain. LANE BORDER: firefly and deep-sea BIOluminescence are the ANIMAL bank's (creature adaptation) -- no rung here may key a living light organ; fireflies may appear only as a one-clause contrast, never as the answer.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank owns bioluminescent creatures (fireflies, anglerfish, dinoflagellates) as adaptations; no rung in this ladder may key a creature's light organ or luciferin/luciferase biology.
